source.title: Empirical Evaluation of Large Language Models in Automated Program Repair
source.authors: Jia-Jun Sun; Feng-Jie Li; Xin Qi; Hong-Yu Zhang; Jia-Jun Jiang

record.tranche_reason: The study compares repair performance across models of different parameter sizes, providing a downstream-task measure relevant to V6. It does not reproduce a held-out-loss scaling-law experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper reports APR outcomes while comparing models of different sizes, so those results bear on downstream predictability (V6). It does not measure pretraining loss, fit power laws, run a controlled size/token/compute sweep, or test compute-optimal allocations. Other reported outcomes, including prompt-setting comparisons, patch rankings, bug-length analyses, and edit-operation counts, do not test the claim versions. Claims and results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study benchmarks four existing LLMs (7B–33B) on program repair and explicitly discusses how repair rate changes with model size. This is a coarse result on V6 in a new setting, automated program repair. Size is confounded with model family, training data and instruction tuning. There is no controlled sweep, no fit, and no link to pretraining loss, so it is a weak T3 test rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say larger models tend to repair better, and that repair does not scale linearly with size, with diminishing returns among code models. They also say fine-tuned CodeLlama-7B beats LLaMA-2-13B on every dataset, and that smaller models fix unique bugs. They stress specialization over scale, early-rank patches and prompt sensitivity. Their prose example (DeepSeek 'only repaired 4 fewer bugs' than CodeLlama) contradicts Table IV, where DeepSeek fixes 4 more.
record.recipe_differences: This is an empirical APR benchmark comparison, not a scaling-law replication: it compares four existing models with different sizes, training, and specialization, and measures repair rates rather than held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Repair performance differs with model specialization and dataset; the paper reports weaker results on BugsCpp and stronger results on several algorithmic-assignment datasets.
record.problems: Only four models are compared, and model size is confounded with architecture, training, and code specialization. The evaluation reports APR repair outcomes rather than scaling-law loss or controlled parameter/token/compute sweeps. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The prose contains a count inconsistency for Defects4J v1.2: it says DeepSeek repaired 4 fewer bugs than CodeLlama, while Table IV reports 44 versus 40.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted among the model-by-dataset repair-rate outcomes in Tables IV and V. Prompt-setting outcomes in Table VI and patch-rank, bug-length, and edit-operation analyses were excluded because they do not compare model scale for V6.

untested.parts: No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fits in other regimes.
Predictability itself: no fitted trend, no relation to pretraining loss, only four uncontrolled model points from different families.

missing.what: Per-model repair rates under the zero-shot and bug-analysis prompts. Under zero-shot the code models order by size: ConDefects-Java 5.0<9.4<21.0; ConDefects-Py 2.7<9.6<16.5. Under bug analysis the ordering breaks on ConDefects-Py: CodeLlama 10.7 > StarCoder 9.1. This bears on whether the size ordering depends on the prompt. rows_left_out wrongly says these rows do not compare scale.

record.verdict_notes: This is an APR benchmark, not a scaling study. There are only four models, from three providers, differing in pretraining data, code specialization and instruction tuning (DeepSeek is instruct). Any 'scale' signal is therefore confounded. No uncertainty is reported, and BugsCpp counts are very small. I downgraded the tranche from the reader's T2 to T3. Row states were reassigned from a blanket 'partial' to states read relative to the other models in each dataset.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
No predictions from smaller runs are compared with larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token growth trend.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
No power-law tests in other modalities or training regimes.

The study measures APR repair rates, not a range of downstream tasks or performance as a function of pretraining loss. Its model comparisons do not isolate parameter count from training and specialization.
No fitted exponents, compute-optimal split, or comparison of scaling-law fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Three code-specialized models (7B, 15.5B, 33B) on Defects4J v2.0, IntroClass-C/Java and ConDefects-Java/Py
relationships.reason: Repair rate rises monotonically with size on these five datasets (r05,r07,r08,r13,r15,r16,r17,r19,r20,r21,r23,r24,r25,r27,r28). This is a coarse ordering across different model families, not a fitted prediction.
relationships.display_finding: Repair rates increased from 7B to 15.5B to 33B on all five datasets, although the models came from different families.

relationships.condition: Code-specialized models on Defects4J v1.2 and BugsCpp (enterprise bugs)
relationships.reason: On Defects4J v1.2, gains are tiny for 4.7x the parameters (15.7→17.3%; r01,r03,r04). On BugsCpp the ordering is non-monotone: CodeLlama-7B 4.7% beats StarCoder-15.5B 2.8% (r09,r11,r12).
relationships.display_finding: A 4.7-fold parameter increase raised Defects4J repair rates only from 15.7% to 17.3%, while CodeLlama-7B beat StarCoder-15.5B on BugsCpp, 4.7% versus 2.8%.

relationships.reason: The larger general model has a lower repair rate on all seven datasets (r02/r01, r06/r05, r10/r09, r14/r13, r18/r17, r22/r21, r26/r25). Training specialization outweighs size; confounded, so not a clean reversal.
relationships.display_finding: LLaMA-2-13B repaired fewer bugs than CodeLlama-7B on all seven datasets, although specialization confounded the size comparison.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The three code-specialized models compared across the seven datasets
reader_labels.reason: The reported repair rates generally rank higher for the larger code-specialized models, with DeepSeek-Coder-33B-instruct highest on each dataset; this is a coarse ordering, not a fitted prediction. Rows r01-r04, r05-r08, r09-r12, r13-r16, r17-r20, r21-r24, and r25-r28.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The smaller, code-fine-tuned CodeLlama has a higher repair rate than the larger general-purpose LLaMA-2-13B on all seven datasets, and the authors state that gains do not scale linearly with model size. Rows r01-r02, r05-r06, r09-r10, r13-r14, r17-r18, r21-r22, and r25-r26.
